claim: OAS1 p46 is an isoform of oligoadenylate synthetase 1 that is prenylated and targeted to the endomembrane system.
source: Here, we reveal that an isoform of oligoadenylate synthetase 1, OAS1 p46, is prenylated and targeted to the endomembrane system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing geranylgeranylation and membrane localization of p46.

claim: Membrane localization of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced access to viral replication sites.
source: Membrane localization of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced access to viral replication sites and results in increased antiviral activity against a subset of RNA viruses including flaviviruses, picornaviruses, and SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing p46 localization to viral replication sites and RNA immunoprecipitation showing enhanced viral RNA binding.

claim: OAS1 p46 has increased antiviral activity against flaviviruses, picornaviruses, and SARS-CoV-2 compared to other OAS1 isoforms.
source: Membrane localization of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced access to viral replication sites and results in increased antiviral activity against a subset of RNA viruses including flaviviruses, picornaviruses, and SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data showing reduced viral replication in cells expressing p46.

claim: The OAS1 splice-site SNP rs10774671 responsible for production of the OAS1 p46 isoform correlates with protection from severe COVID-19.
source: Finally, our human genetic analysis shows that the OAS1 splice-site SNP responsible for production of the OAS1 p46 isoform correlates with protection from severe COVID-19.
evidence: Supported by genetic association data from COVID-19 patient cohorts.

claim: OAS proteins are a family of interferon-induced sensors of viral RNA critical for cell-intrinsic innate immune defense against viruses through activation of RNase L.
source: Oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS) proteins are a family of interferon (IFN)-induced sensors of viral RNA critical for cell-intrinsic innate immune defense against viruses through activation of the latent endoribonuclease RNase L (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Recognition of viral dsRNA induces a conformational change in OAS proteins to reveal a catalytic pocket which converts ATP to 2′−5′A.
source: Recognition of viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) induces a conformational change in OAS proteins to reveal a catalytic pocket which converts ATP to the second messenger 2′−5′A (Lohöfener et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Binding to 2′−5′A dimerizes and activates RNase L, which cleaves cellular and viral RNA to block viral replication.
source: Binding to 2′−5′A dimerizes and activates RNase L, which cleaves cellular and viral RNA in order to block viral replication (Han et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The C-terminal region of human OAS1 is alternatively spliced to produce protein isoforms p42, p44, p46, p48, and p52.
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal region of human OAS1 is alternatively spliced to produce the protein isoforms p42, p44, p46, p48, and p52, named according to their molecular weight (Bonnevie-Nielsen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: All human OAS1 isoforms share the first five exons of OAS1, which contain the RNA binding and catalytic domains.
source: All human OAS1 isoforms share the first five exons of OAS1, which contain the RNA binding and catalytic domains, but each isoform splices a distinct sixth exon to generate unique C-termini.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The production of OAS1 p46 is controlled by an SNP in the splice-acceptor site of exon six in OAS1 (rs10774671 A>G).
source: The production of OAS1 p46 is controlled by an SNP in the splice-acceptor site of exon six in OAS1 (rs10774671 A>G) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data and protein expression analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The G allele of rs10774671 shifts the splice acceptor site in exon 6 by one nucleotide to generate p46, while the A allele produces primarily p42.
source: The G allele of this SNP shifts the splice acceptor site in exon 6 by one nucleotide to generate p46, while other OAS1 isoforms, primarily p42, are produced when the A allele is present (Lim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data showing isoform expression patterns.

claim: OAS1 p46 is unique among OAS1 isoforms because it is the only isoform with a C-terminal CaaX motif.
source: OAS1 p46 is unique among OAS1 isoforms because it is the only isoform with a C-terminal CaaX (cysteine-aliphatic-aliphatic-any residue) motif.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Proteins containing CaaX motifs undergo prenylation and are targeted to intracellular organelle membranes of the endomembrane system.
source: Proteins containing CaaX motifs at their C-termini undergo a post translational lipidation modification termed prenylation and are targeted to the cytosolic face of intracellular organelle membranes of the endomembrane system following post-prenylation processing at the endoplasmic reticulum (Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on protein prenylation.

claim: The splice site SNP rs10774671 in OAS1 is associated with genetic susceptibility to multiple flaviviruses and autoimmune disorders.
source: This splice site SNP in OAS1 is associated with genetic susceptibility to multiple flaviviruses and autoimmune disorders (El Awady et al., 2011; Haralambieva et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Simon-Loriere et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple genetic association studies.

claim: Most positive-strand RNA viruses replicate within a modified organelle co-opted from intracellular membranes of the endomembrane system.
source: However, most positive-strand RNA viruses replicate within a modified organelle co-opted from intracellular membranes of the endomembrane system, which shields viral products from cellular innate immune sensors.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of positive-strand RNA virus replication strategies.

claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses such as flaviviruses, picornaviruses, and coronaviruses replicate their RNA within modified host organelles of the endomembrane system.
source: Notably, positive-strand RNA viruses, such as flaviviruses, picornaviruses, and coronaviruses replicate their RNA within modified host organelles of the endomembrane system (Romero-Brey and Bartenschlager, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on virus replication.

claim: Replication organelles shield viral RNA from detection by cytosolic RNA sensors such as RIG-I.
source: These replication organelles shield vRNA from detection by cytosolic RNA sensors such as RIG-I (Neufeldt et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on viral immune evasion.

claim: OAS1 p46 is geranylgeranylated at its C-terminal CaaX motif.
source: Immunoblotting of the immunoprecipitated OAS1 proteins revealed CaaX-containing p46 and p42CTIL proteins were geranylgeranylated, while p42 and p46ATIL were not (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by click chemistry assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The CaaX motif is both necessary and sufficient for the geranylgeranylation of OAS1.
source: These data confirm that p46, but not p42, is geranylgeranylated and demonstrate that the CaaX motif is both necessary and sufficient for the geranylgeranylation of OAS1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing p46, p42, p42CTIL, and p46ATIL geranylgeranylation.

claim: OAS1 p46 localizes to the trans-Golgi network in cells producing this isoform.
source: Co-staining with Golgin-97 identified that OAS1 was predominantly localized at the trans-Golgi network in p46-producing cells (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization with Golgin-97.

claim: OAS1 p42 localizes to the cytosol and nucleus.
source: In contrast, OAS1 localized to the cytosol and nucleus in cells incapable of producing p46 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: The CaaX motif is necessary for the Golgi localization of OAS1 p46.
source: p46ATIL localized to the cytosol and nucleus, similar to p42, indicating the CaaX motif is necessary for the Golgi localization of p46 (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing p46ATIL localization.

claim: The CaaX motif is sufficient to localize OAS1 isoforms to the Golgi.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, ectopically expressed p42CTIL localized to the Golgi and showed significantly stronger co-localization with the Golgi over p42, confirming the CaaX motif is both necessary and sufficient to localize OAS1 isoforms to the Golgi (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing p42CTIL localization.

claim: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against EMCV compared to p42.
source: We found p42 expression led to a significant fivefold reduction in EMCV RNA over control, while p46 expression led to a significant 50-fold reduction over EV and a significant 10-fold reduction over p42 at 24 hr post-infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and plaque assay data.

claim: OAS1 p46 reduces EMCV titer by 100-fold compared to control and 50-fold compared to p42.
source: Quantification of viral titer from supernatants by plaque assay showed p46 expression led to a significant 100-fold reduction in EMCV titer over control and a significant 50-fold reduction over p42.
evidence: Supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Depletion of OAS1 p46 in THP-1 cells leads to increased EMCV titer.
source: Depletion of total OAS1 or p46 led to a significant four-fold increase in viral titer compared to a non-targeting control (NC), whereas specific knockdown of p42 had no effect on viral titer compared to NC siRNA (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and viral titer measurements.

claim: Primary human fibroblasts with at least one copy of the G allele at rs10774671 have reduced EMCV burden.
source: Quantification of EMCV RNA and viral titer at 24 hr post-infection revealed that cells with at least one copy of the G allele had reduced levels of EMCV burden (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Supported by experiments in primary human fibroblasts from donors with different genotypes.

claim: Catalytic activity is essential for both OAS1 p42 and p46 to restrict EMCV.
source: As before, expression of p42 and p46 reduced EMCV RNA and titer to different degrees. However, the catalytically inactive OAS1 constructs failed to restrict EMCV RNA or titer (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by experiments using catalytic mutants of p42 and p46.

claim: The ability to synthesize 2′−5′A is essential for both OAS1 p42 and p46 to restrict EMCV.
source: These data indicate that the ability to synthesize 2′−5′A is essential for both OAS1 p42 and p46 to restrict EMCV.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing catalytic mutants lack antiviral activity.

claim: RNase L is required for the antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 and p46 against EMCV.
source: Compared to non-targeted Cas9 control cells, expression of p42 and p46 in RNASEL KO 293 T cells had no impact on EMCV vRNA or titers (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by experiments in RNase L knockout cells.

claim: These experiments show that RNase L is required for the antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 and p46 against EMCV.
source: These experiments show that RNase L is required for the antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 and p46 against EMCV.
evidence: Supported by RNase L knockout and complementation experiments.

claim: OAS1 p42 and p46 share a similar capacity to synthesize 2′−5′A.
source: As expected, these isoforms shared a similar capacity to synthesize 2′−5′A and the CaaX motif did not alter the catalytic activity (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by in vitro 2′−5′A synthesis assay data.

claim: The CaaX motif does not alter the catalytic activity of OAS1.
source: As expected, these isoforms shared a similar capacity to synthesize 2′−5′A and the CaaX motif did not alter the catalytic activity (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by in vitro 2′−5′A synthesis assay comparing p42, p46, and CaaX mutants.

claim: Loss of IRF3 expression does not impede the ability of p46 to restrict EMCV.
source: Importantly, loss of IRF3 expression did not impede the ability of p46 to restrict EMCV, as EMCV RNA was significantly reduced over control in IRF3 KO cells expressing p46 (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by experiments in IRF3 knockout cells.

claim: OAS1 p42 and p46 confer antiviral activity in the absence of additional factors induced by IRF3.
source: These data confirm p42 and p46 confer antiviral activity in the absence of additional factors that are induced by IRF3.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing antiviral activity in IRF3 knockout cells.

claim: OAS1 p46 redistributes to sites of EMCV dsRNA replication during infection.
source: In cells infected with EMCV, p46 was no longer perinuclear and instead redistributed throughout the cell to sites of double-stranded viral RNA replication intermediate accumulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data during EMCV infection.

claim: OAS1 p42 remains in the cytosol and nucleus before and after EMCV infection.
source: In contrast, p42 remained in the cytosol and nucleus before and after infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data during EMCV infection.

claim: OAS1 p46 has enhanced access to EMCV RNA compared to p42.
source: RT-qPCR for EMCV RNA after FLAG immunoprecipitation revealed that p46 tended to bind more EMCV RNA than p42 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Mutating the CaaX motif on p46 causes a significant loss in EMCV RNA binding.
source: Although adding a CaaX motif to p42 (p42CTIL) did not significantly increase the ability of p42 to pull down EMCV RNA, mutating the CaaX motif on p46 (p46ATIL) caused a significant loss in EMCV RNA binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Endomembrane targeting through the CaaX motif is required for p46 to bind EMCV RNA.
source: These data confirm that endomembrane targeting through the CaaX motif is required for p46 to bind EMCV RNA, as mutating the CaaX motif completely ablated the ability of p46 to access EMCV RNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation data showing loss of binding in p46ATIL.

claim: Cells expressing CaaX-mutant p46ATIL show increased EMCV RNA and titer compared to cells expressing p46.
source: Compared to cells expressing p46, cells expressing CaaX-mutant p46ATIL showed a significant five-fold increase in EMCV RNA as well as an increase in viral titer; a decreased antiviral activity similar to that of the p42 isoform (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA and titer quantification data.

claim: Addition of a CaaX motif to OAS1 p42 does not increase its antiviral activity.
source: Intriguingly, addition of a CaaX motif to OAS1 p42 did not increase the antiviral activity of p42 (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA and titer data for p42CTIL.

claim: Membrane targeting of OAS1 p46 through a CaaX motif is crucial for its antiviral activity against EMCV.
source: Together, these data indicate membrane targeting of OAS1 p46 through a CaaX motif is crucial for its antiviral activity against EMCV.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing loss of antiviral activity when CaaX motif is mutated.

claim: A CaaX motif alone is not sufficient to provide optimal antiviral activity against EMCV.
source: However, a CaaX motif alone is not sufficient to provide optimal antiviral activity against EMCV.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing p42CTIL does not have enhanced antiviral activity.

claim: The CFK motif is critical for OAS1 oligomerization and 2′−5′A production.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated a three amino acid motif (C331F332K333), present in all OAS1 isoforms, is critical for OAS1 oligomerization and 2′−5′A production (Ghosh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Mutation of the CFK domain leads to loss of antiviral activity in both p42 and p46.
source: Relative to wild type p42 and p46, mutation of the CFK domain led to a significant loss in the ability of p42 and p46 to reduce EMCV RNA by threefold and twofold, respectively (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for CFK mutants.

claim: Disruption of the CFK motif in p42 results in complete loss of antiviral activity.
source: Interestingly, disruption of the CFK motif in p42 resulted in complete loss of antiviral activity, demonstrated by similar EMCV RNA copies as cells expressing an empty vector control (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claim: OAS1 p46 with a disrupted CFK motif maintains residual antiviral activity similar to wild-type p42.
source: OAS1 p46 with a disrupted CFK motif maintained residual antiviral activity similar to the antiviral activity of wild-type p42 (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claim: The antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 is completely dependent on the CFK oligomerization motif.
source: This suggests that the antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 is completely dependent on the CFK oligomerization motif, whereas p46 only partially depends on the CFK oligomerization motif for its antiviral activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments comparing CFK mutants of p42 and p46.

claim: OAS1 p46 only partially depends on the CFK oligomerization motif for its antiviral activity.
source: This suggests that the antiviral activity of OAS1 p42 is completely dependent on the CFK oligomerization motif, whereas p46 only partially depends on the CFK oligomerization motif for its antiviral activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments comparing CFK mutants of p42 and p46.

claim: C-terminal truncation mutants of p46 show a length-dependent decrease in their ability to reduce EMCV RNA.
source: Compared to p46, the truncation mutants showed a length-dependent decrease in their ability to reduce EMCV RNA (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for truncation mutants.

claim: The C-terminal length of p46 is important for its antiviral activity.
source: These data suggest that, in addition to the CaaX motif and an oligomerization domain, the C-terminal length of p46 is important for its antiviral activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with C-terminal truncation mutants.

claim: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against West Nile virus compared to p42.
source: Expression of p46 led to a 90% reduction in WNV titer relative to control, while p42 did not significantly impact WNV titer (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by viral titer quantification data.

claim: OAS1 p46 localizes to PDIA3 and dsRNA-positive WNV replication sites during infection.
source: However, during WNV infection, p46 localized to PDIA3 and dsRNA-positive replication sites (Figure 6B, bottom panel, arrows).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data during WNV infection.

claim: OAS1 p42 does not appear to be recruited to sites of WNV RNA production during infection.
source: During WNV infection, we observed p42 in the cytosol and nucleus. Indeed, p42 did not appear to be recruited to sites of WNV RNA production (Figure 6B, top panel, arrows).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data during WNV infection.

claim: OAS1 p46 has significantly stronger localization to dsRNA during WNV infection than p42.
source: Quantification of OAS1 isoform localization to viral RNA revealed OAS1 p46 has significantly stronger localization to dsRNA during WNV infection than p42 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claim: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against CVB3 compared to p42.
source: RT-qPCR analysis at 24 hr post-infection revealed a 70% reduction in CVB3 RNA in p46 expressing cells compared to control, while p42 had almost no effect on CVB3 RNA levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). Similarly, CVB3 titers at 48 hr post-infection were significantly reduced by 50% in p46 expressing cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA and titer quantification data.

claim: OAS1 p46 has enhanced antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2 compared to p42.
source: Expression of p42 led to a fivefold reduction in SARS-CoV-2 titer (Figure 6F). However, p46 had a significant fivefold greater antiviral activity over p42 (25-fold over EV) against SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by viral titer quantification data.

claim: The enhanced antiviral activity of p46 against SARS-CoV-2 depends on the CaaX motif.
source: Importantly, the enhanced antiviral activity of p46 against SARS-CoV-2 depended on the CaaX motif, as p46ATIL demonstrated decreased antiviral activity similar to that of p42.
evidence: Supported by viral titer data for p46ATIL shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Endomembrane targeting of p46 is critical to its enhanced antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2.
source: This suggests that endomembrane targeting of p46 is critical to its enhanced antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing loss of activity in p46ATIL.

claim: OAS1 p42 and p46 do not significantly impact IAV RNA levels.
source: Viral RNA analysis revealed neither OAS1 isoform impacted IAV RNA levels significantly at 24 hr post-infection.
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Expression of p42 or p46 has no impact on the replication of NS1-mutant IAV.
source: We found that expression of p42 or p46 had no impact on the replication of this NS1-mutant IAV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by viral titer data.

claim: GFP-expressing VSV is insensitive to OAS1 p42 and p46.
source: Similarly, we observed that GFP-expressing VSV, which replicates in the cytosol, was also insensitive to OAS1 p42 and p46. Compared to an empty vector control, expression of p42 or p46 did not impact the number of GFP+ cells during infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: OAS1 p46 is broadly antiviral against viruses that use the endomembrane system for replication.
source: Collectively, these data suggest OAS1 p46 is broadly antiviral against viruses that use the endomembrane system for replication.
evidence: Inferred from antiviral activity data against multiple positive-strand RNA viruses.

claim: The G allele at rs10774671 is associated with protection from severe COVID-19.
source: We detected association of rs10774671 in severe COVID-19 cases (p=0.017, Odds Ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.15–0.83) using a dominant model, indicating that the G allele was protective for severe COVID-19 disease (Supplementary file 5 and Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by genetic association analysis in COVID-19 patient cohorts.

claim: Significant association of the rs10774671 G allele with severe COVID-19 was detected in a replication cohort (p=7.38x10−7, OR 0.80 95% CI 0.71–0.89).
source: Significant association of the rs10774671 G allele with severe COVID-19 was detected (p=7.38x10−7, OR 0.80 95% CI 0.71–0.89).
evidence: Supported by genetic association analysis in UK cohorts.

claim: The G allele at OAS1 rs10774671 encoding the OAS1 p46 isoform contributes protection from severe disease in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients.
source: Together these results demonstrate that the G allele at OAS1 rs10774671 encoding the OAS1 p46 isoform contributes protection from severe disease in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients.
evidence: Inferred from genetic association data and in vitro antiviral activity data.

claim: Endomembrane targeting of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced antiviral activity against viruses that use the endomembrane system for their replication.
source: In this study, we show that endomembrane targeting of OAS1 p46 confers enhanced antiviral activity against viruses that use the endomembrane system for their replication.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing enhanced antiviral activity of p46 against positive-strand RNA viruses.

claim: Localizing OAS1 p46 to the endomembrane system results in enhanced access to viral RNA and activation of RNase L dependent antiviral activity.
source: Although replicating in these modified endomembrane compartments is an important immune evasion strategy of positive-strand RNA viruses, out data shows localizing OAS1 p46 to the endomembrane system results in enhanced access to viral RNA and activation of RNase L dependent antiviral activity.
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and antiviral activity data.

claim: OAS1 p42 has a comparatively weak ability to sense viral RNA and initiate antiviral activity against viruses that replicate within intracellular membranes.
source: In contrast, p42, which is localized to the cytosol and nucleus, has a comparatively weak ability to sense viral RNA and initiate antiviral activity against viruses that replicate within intracellular membranes (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by comparative antiviral activity data between p42 and p46.

claim: Placement of innate immune sensors at intracellular membranes is an antiviral strategy difficult for positive-strand RNA viruses to evade.
source: Placement of innate immune sensors at intracellular membranes is an antiviral strategy likely difficult for positive-strand RNA viruses to evade, as these viruses are unlikely to evolve away from this fundamental replication strategy.
evidence: Based on speculation about viral evolution and replication strategies.

claim: Prenylated OAS1 p46 localizes to the cytosolic surface of the organelle membrane.
source: Based on our data, we propose that prenylated OAS1 p46 localizes to the cytosolic surface of the organelle membrane.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental data and knowledge of prenylation.

claim: During infection with a positive-strand RNA virus, viral non-structural proteins and viral RNA are recruited to the organelle surface where p46 can interact with vRNA.
source: During infection with a positive-strand RNA virus, the viral non-structural proteins and viral RNA are recruited to the organelle surface, where p46 can interact with vRNA.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental observations and knowledge of virus replication.

claim: As the membrane is involuted to form the viral replication organelle, prenylated p46 is also included in the VRO.
source: As the membrane is involuted to form the viral replication organelle (VRO), prenylated p46 is also included in the VRO.
evidence: Based on speculation about VRO formation and p46 localization.

claim: Confinement of p46 in the VRO may enhance its access to viral RNA.
source: Confinement of p46 in the VRO may enhance its access to viral RNA.
evidence: Based on speculation about the consequences of p46 localization.

claim: Many positive-strand RNA viruses depend on lipid products of the mevalonate pathway or prenylation for replication.
source: Secondly, many positive-strand RNA viruses depend on lipid products of the mevalonate pathway or prenylation for replication and therefore cannot broadly antagonize this pathway (Mackenzie et al., 2007; Romero-Brey and Bartenschlager, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The rs10774671 G allele controlling OAS1 p46 expression was originally identified as a West Nile virus resistance allele.
source: The rs10774671 G allele controlling OAS1 p46 expression was originally identified as a West Nile virus resistance allele, although the mechanism accounting for the protection conferred by this SNP was lacking (Lim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous genetic association study.

claim: The A allele at rs10774671 contributes to genetic risk for severe COVID-19 disease in patients with respiratory failure.
source: We found the A allele contributes to genetic risk for severe COVID-19 disease in patients with respiratory failure compared to healthy control subjects in two cohorts.
evidence: Supported by genetic association data from two cohorts.

claim: The G allele association with protection against severe COVID-19 is explained by the enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46 against SARS-CoV-2.
source: We propose that the G allele association with protection against severe COVID-19 is explained by the enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46 against SARS-CoV-2, which contributes to early control of viral replication.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic association and in vitro antiviral activity data.

claim: Both rs10774671 and the lead GWAS SNP rs10735079 are expression and splicing QTL for OAS1 and OAS3.
source: Additionally, both rs10774671 and the lead GWAS SNP rs10735079 are expression and splicing QTL for OAS1 and OAS3 in our analyses (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to genetic analysis.

claim: The association of rs10774671 and rs10735079 with severe COVID-19 may affect both splicing and expression levels of OAS1 and OAS3.
source: Thus, the association of these SNPs with severe COVID-19 may be two-fold: affecting splicing and expression levels both of those observed in primary human cells.
evidence: Based on inference from QTL analysis.

claim: The G allele is ancestral and prevalent in African populations.
source: Interestingly, the G allele is ancestral and prevalent in African populations.
evidence: Supported by population genetics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The A allele is prevalent in the rest of the world outside of Africa.
source: In contrast, the A allele is prevalent in rest of the world (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by population genetics data.

claim: The G-allele was reintroduced into Homo sapiens population by introgression from Neanderthals.
source: Previous studies have documented reintroduction of the G-allele into Homo sapiens population by introgression from Neanderthals (Sams et al., 2016), and this could have implications for COVID-19 disease.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous genetic study.

claim: IFNAR2 and TYK2 are innate immune genes upstream of OAS1 that are associated with severe COVID-19.
source: Other innate immune genes upstream of OAS1 that are associated with severe COVID-19 in a genome wide association study are IFNAR2, and TYK2, which are in the type I IFN pathway (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to GWAS study.

claim: Perturbations in IFNAR2 or TYK2 could affect OAS1 expression and its effector activity.
source: Perturbations in any of these genes could affect OAS1 expression and its effector activity.
evidence: Based on inference from knowledge of the IFN pathway.

claim: The type I IFN pathway might be compromised in patients with severe COVID-19.
source: Genetic studies, SARS-CoV-2 antagonism of IFN transcription, and autoantibodies against IFNα/β strongly associate with severe COVID-19, indicating that the type I IFN pathway might be compromised in patients with severe COVID-19 (Bastard et al., 2021; de Prost et al., 2021; Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on COVID-19 and IFN.

claim: There are strong selective pressures, presumably viral, impacting the prevalence of OAS1 causal splice site-SNP in human populations.
source: While it would be interesting to study the individual and combined effects of the above genes on OAS1 and COVID-19 disease, our study suggests there are strong selective pressures, presumably viral, impacting the prevalence of OAS1 causal splice site-SNP in in human populations. (Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on inference from genetic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The OAS family in humans is comprised of three catalytically active OAS proteins: OAS1, OAS2, and OAS3.
source: In humans, the OAS family is comprised of three catalytically active OAS proteins: OAS1, OAS2, and OAS3.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the OAS family.

claim: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain.
source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of the OAS1 unit.
source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of the OAS1 unit.
source: OAS1 contains an RNA binding domain and a catalytically active domain, while OAS2 contains a catalytically inactive repeat of this unit, and OAS3 contains two catalytically inactive repeats of this unit (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A.
source: Although the OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A (Ibsen et al., 2014), we demonstrate a novel mechanism where subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of these proteins.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of OAS proteins.
source: Although the OAS proteins have different RNA binding capabilities and favor synthesis of different lengths of 2′−5′A (Ibsen et al., 2014), we demonstrate a novel mechanism where subcellular localization determines the antiviral specificity of these proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential antiviral activity based on localization.

claim: 2′−5′A locally activates RNase L around sites of viral replication.
source: Based on the reduction of vRNA in our study, we propose a model in which 2′−5′A locally activates RNase L around sites of viral replication.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental observations.

claim: The A allele at rs10774671 is associated with multiple autoimmune disorders.
source: This is further supported by the genetic association of the A allele with multiple autoimmune disorders, as enhanced immune responses are sometimes made at a tradeoff for overall host fitness (Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: By positioning viral RNA sensors at different subcellular sites, the host can potentially respond to diverse replication strategies.
source: By positioning viral RNA sensors at different subcellular sites of viral RNA accumulation, the host can potentially respond to diverse replication strategies in the cytosol, nucleus, or on intracellular membranes.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and knowledge of viral replication.

claim: Subcellular targeting is likely important for function of other OAS proteins.
source: Although this work focused on OAS1 and the detection of viral nucleic acids, subcellular targeting is likely also important for function of other OAS proteins.
evidence: Based on speculation from findings about OAS1.

claim: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini.
source: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini, suggesting the CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 across vertebrate species.
source: OAS1 proteins from diverse vertebrate species have a CaaX motif at their C-termini, suggesting the CaaX motif has a conserved role in the function of OAS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from conservation of CaaX motif across species.

claim: The A549 cell line carries only the A allele at rs10774671.
source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claim: PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carry both the A and G alleles at rs10774671.
source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claim: Daudi cells carry only the G allele at rs10774671.
source: Genotyping revealed that the A549 cell line carried only the A allele, that PH5CH8 and THP-1 cell lines carried both the A and G alleles, and that Daudi cells carried only the G allele at rs10774671 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data.

claim: Two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa were detected in cells with at least one copy of the G allele.
source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Only p42 is expressed in A/A cells at rs10774671.
source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Only p46 is expressed in G/G cells at rs10774671.
source: We detected two OAS1 isoforms at molecular weights of 42 and 46 kDa in cells with at least one copy of the G allele, while only p42 or p46 were expressed in A/A or G/G cells, respectively (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data.

claim: The p44, p48, and p52 isoforms were not observed under the experimental conditions used.
source: We did not observe the expression of other OAS1 isoforms under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing only p42 and p46.

claim: Cells homozygous for the A allele at rs10774671 only produce p42.
source: Cells homozygous for the A allele only produced p42, while cells homozygous for the G allele only produced p46 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claim: Cells homozygous for the G allele at rs10774671 only produce p46.
source: Cells homozygous for the A allele only produced p42, while cells homozygous for the G allele only produced p46 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claim: PBMCs harboring at least one G allele express p46 stronger than p42.
source: Corroborating our findings, PBMCs harboring at least one G allele expressed p46 stronger than p42, which may be influenced by splice site preference or mRNA stability.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from PBMCs.

claim: The p44, p48, and p52 isoforms are weakly expressed at the mRNA level and unstable at the protein level.
source: We did not observe expression of the p44, p48, or p52 isoforms in any of the cells used in this study, which is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that these isoforms are weakly expressed at the mRNA level, and unstable at the protein level (Carey et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CaaX motifs with a leucine in the 'X' position are preferentially geranylgeranylated by GGTaseI.
source: Depending on the identity of the 'X' amino acid, CaaX-containing proteins can be either farnesylated or geranylgeranylated by the respective farnesyl or geranylgeranyl transferases. CaaX motifs with a leucine in the 'X' position, as in the case of p46, are preferentially geranylgeranylated by geranylgeranyl transferase I (GGTaseI) (Hartman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on prenylation.

claim: EMCV is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family that replicates on ER and Golgi membranes.
source: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family, which replicates on organelles of the endomembrane system, particularly ER and Golgi membranes, and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Chebath et al., 1987; Melia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: EMCV is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway.
source: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is a positive-strand RNA virus in the picornavirus family, which replicates on organelles of the endomembrane system, particularly ER and Golgi membranes, and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Chebath et al., 1987; Melia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The antiviral activity of p44, p48, and p52 against EMCV is inferior to p46.
source: We also compared the antiviral activity of p44, p48, and p52 against EMCV over a range of doses and found their antiviral activity was inferior to p46 (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claim: Among OAS1 isoforms, OAS1 p46 confers the strongest antiviral activity against EMCV.
source: These data demonstrate that, among OAS1 isoforms, OAS1 p46 confers the strongest antiviral activity against EMCV.
evidence: Inferred from comparative antiviral activity data across all isoforms.

claim: Complementing RNASEL KO cells with RNase L and p46 significantly reduces EMCV RNA and titer.
source: RNASEL KO 293 T cells complemented with RNase L and expressing p46 showed a significant reduction in EMCV RNA and titer over control.
evidence: Supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E and F.

claim: Cleavage of cellular RNA by RNase L generates immunostimulatory RNAs that are sensed by RIG-I and MDA5.
source: Cleavage of cellular RNA by RNase L has been shown to generate immunostimulatory RNAs that are sensed by RIG-I and MDA5 and increase antiviral protection through the production of interferon (Malathi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: During picornavirus infection, ER- and Golgi-derived membranes form replication organelles that are sites of vRNA replication.
source: During picornavirus infection, ER- and Golgi-derived membranes form replication organelles that are sites of vRNA replication (Melia et al., 2019; Melia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Endomembrane localization of p46 places this viral RNA sensor on membranes utilized by EMCV for replication.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that endomembrane localization of p46 places this viral RNA sensor on membranes utilized by EMCV for replication and would allow the enhanced access of p46 to EMCV RNA.
evidence: Based on hypothesis from knowledge of EMCV replication and p46 localization.

claim: OAS1 p46 is in close proximity to sites of EMCV RNA replication where dsRNA ligands are present.
source: These data suggest that p46 is in close proximity to sites of EMCV RNA replication where dsRNA ligands are present.
evidence: Inferred from microscopy data showing p46 colocalization with dsRNA.

claim: OAS1 common+CTIL does not confer significantly increased antiviral activity over empty vector control.
source: At similar protein expression levels, OAS1 common+CTIL did not confer significantly increased antiviral activity over the empty vector control and showed RNA levels similar to those in cells expressing the p42 isoform (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claim: OAS1 common+CTIL shows significantly decreased co-localization with Golgi membranes compared to p46.
source: Interestingly, the OAS1 common+CTIL variant showed significantly decreased co-localization with Golgi membranes compared to p46 and appeared cytosolic and nuclear, as observed above for CaaX-deficient p42 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: Other features in the unique C-termini of OAS1 p42 and p46 contribute to their individual antiviral activity.
source: Overall, these data suggest other features in the unique C-termini of OAS1 p42 and p46 contribute to their individual antiviral activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing CaaX motif alone is not sufficient.

claim: None of the alanine substitution mutants in the p46 C-terminus affected viral RNA levels as strongly as disruption of the CaaX motif.
source: Nevertheless, none of the alanine substitution mutants affected EMCV RNA levels as strongly as the disruption of the CaaX motif in p46ATIL.
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for alanine mutants.

claim: The E392-E/N393-D/N394 sequence is conserved in most mammalian OAS1 p46 orthologous isoforms.
source: In fact, the E392-E/N393-D/N394 sequence is conserved in most mammalian OAS1 p46 orthologous isoforms, which suggests a possible function for this motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: OAS1 p46 mutant eight shows a slight but significant decrease in co-localization with Golgin-97 compared to p46.
source: Although OAS1 p46 mutant eight localized to the Golgi, compared with p46, this mutant showed a slight but significant decrease in its co-localization with Golgin-97 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: Tetramerization of OAS1 has been proposed as a requirement for synthesis of 2′−5′A.
source: Tetramerization of OAS1 has been proposed as a requirement for synthesis of the second messenger 2′−5′A, indicating that several OAS1 molecules in close proximity are required to induce 2′−5′A synthesis upon viral RNA binding and to subsequently activate the RNase L pathway (Ghosh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: CFK-mediated oligomerization is required for optimal EMCV RNA binding of OAS1 p46.
source: Furthermore, we found that CFK-mediated oligomerization is required for optimal EMCV RNA binding of OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Mutation of the CFK motif does not alter the localization of p42 or p46.
source: Importantly, mutation of the CFK motif did not alter the localization of either isoform (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: The Δ22aa and Δ32aa deletion mutants have similar antiviral activities as p42CTIL.
source: The Δ22aa and Δ32aa deletion mutants had similar antiviral activities as p42CTIL, which is identical in length to the Δ32aa mutant (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data.

claim: All p46 truncation mutants localize to the Golgi.
source: Similar to p46, all the p46 truncation mutants localized to the Golgi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: There is a slight but significant decrease in the correlation of p46 Δ32aa with the Golgi.
source: However, there was a slight but significant decrease in the correlation of p46 Δ32aa with the Golgi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claim: The length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence is important for its antiviral activity.
source: These data are consistent with our hypothesis that the length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence is important for increased antiviral activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with chimeric proteins from different species.

claim: Cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimic human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity.
source: We found cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimicked human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity, whereas the shorter C-terminus of flying fox led to decreased antiviral activity of the chimeric protein compared to human OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claim: The shorter C-terminus of flying fox OAS1 leads to decreased antiviral activity compared to human OAS1 p46.
source: We found cow and fox OAS1 chimeras mimicked human OAS1 p46 antiviral activity, whereas the shorter C-terminus of flying fox led to decreased antiviral activity of the chimeric protein compared to human OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claim: The alligator OAS1 p46 chimeric protein fails to exhibit similar antiviral activity as human OAS1 p46.
source: Intriguingly, the alligator OAS1 p46 chimeric protein, with similar C-terminus length as human p46 but with most divergence in peptide sequence, failed to exhibit similar antiviral activity as human OAS1 p46 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by viral RNA quantification data for chimeric proteins.

claim: The alligator and guinea pig lack conservation of the E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif proximal to the CaaX motif.
source: Upon close examination, we found that the alligator (and guinea pig) lack conservation of the E392-E/N393-D/N394 motif proximal to the CaaX motif, which we have shown is required for strong antiviral activity (Figure 5A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence, CFK oligomerization domain, and potentially E-E/N-D/N sequence are required for enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46.
source: These data suggest that the length of the p46-specific C-terminal sequence, CFK oligomerization domain, and potentially E-E/N-D/N sequence are required for enhanced antiviral activity of OAS1 p46.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments testing different C-terminal features.

claim: West Nile virus replicates on membranes of the endomembrane system, primarily ER-derived membranes.
source: WNV, like all flaviviruses, replicates on membranes of the endomembrane system, primarily ER-derived membranes (Westaway et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: OAS1 p46 is recruited to sites of WNV replication.
source: Quantification of OAS1 isoforms relative to PDIA3 revealed a significant increase in the correlation of p46, but not p42, to PDIA3-positive membranes during infection, suggesting that p46 is recruited to sites of WNV replication (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claim: WNV infection causes a significant decrease in the association of p46 with Golgin-97.
source: OAS1 p46 was significantly more correlated with the Golgi than p42 in both uninfected and WNV-infected cells. However, WNV infection caused a significant decrease in the association of p46 with Golgin-97 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis from microscopy data.

claim: OAS1 p46 may be recruited from the Golgi to sites of WNV replication.
source: This suggests that p46 may be recruited from the Golgi to sites of WNV replication and is consistent with previous observations that Golgi membranes and proteins, including RNA binding proteins, are recruited to the replication organelles of flaviviruses (Ward et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on inference from microscopy data and citation to previous literature.

claim: OAS1 p46 localizes to ZIKV replication sites at the ER.
source: We observed p46, but not p42, localized to ZIKV replication sites at the ER (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data during ZIKV infection.

claim: Endomembrane localization of OAS1 p46 allows this protein to access sites of flavivirus RNA replication.
source: Overall, these data suggest that endomembrane localization of OAS1 p46 allows this protein to access sites of flavivirus RNA replication.
evidence: Inferred from microscopy data showing p46 localization to WNV and ZIKV replication sites.

claim: CVB3 replicates within modified Golgi membranes.
source: The human pathogenic picornavirus coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) replicates within modified Golgi membranes, and thus p46 may also be positioned to readily sense CVB3 RNA (Melia et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: OAS1 p46 may have broad antiviral activity against members of the picornavirus family.
source: These data suggest that OAS1 p46 may have broad antiviral activity against members of the picornavirus family, while p42 is less effective.
evidence: Inferred from antiviral activity data against EMCV and CVB3.

claim: Coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 use the endomembrane system for replication using primarily ER-derived membranes.
source: Coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2 use the endomembrane system for replication using primarily ER-derived membranes (Romero-Brey and Bartenschlager, 2014; Snijder et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IAV replicates within the nucleus.
source: IAV replicates within the nucleus where p42 is also present and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Li et al., 2016; Min and Krug, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IAV is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway.
source: IAV replicates within the nucleus where p42 is also present and is sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway (Li et al., 2016; Min and Krug, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Mutations in IAV NS1 disrupting RNA binding render this virus sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway.
source: Mutations in IAV NS1 disrupting RNA binding render this virus sensitive to the OAS/RNase L pathway, although it is unclear what antiviral role OAS1 isoforms play during IAV infection (Min and Krug, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: VSV replicates in the cytosol.
source: Similarly, we observed that GFP-expressing VSV, which replicates in the cytosol, was also insensitive to OAS1 p42 and p46.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of VSV replication.

claim: The lead SNP rs10735079 in the OAS1/OAS2/OAS3 locus is in high linkage disequilibrium with rs10774671.
source: The lead SNP in this region, rs10735079 (p=1.65x10−8, OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.18–1.42), is in high linkage disequilibrium with the rs10774671 A/G splicing site variant (D'0.91, r2=0.79).
evidence: Supported by linkage disequilibrium analysis.

claim: Newly prenylated proteins are continuously recruited to the organelle surface during infection.
source: Furthermore, newly prenylated proteins are continuously recruited to the organelle surface during infection, which may allow for additional interference of vRNA as it escapes the replication organelle.
evidence: Based on speculation about protein trafficking during infection.

claim: Viral antagonism by specifically targeting OAS1 p46 protein or directly blocking its prenylation or splicing could be possible.
source: Viral antagonism by specifically targeting OAS1 p46 protein or directly blocking its prenylation or splicing could be possible.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential viral evasion mechanisms.

claim: Viral interference of the OAS-RNase L pathway would negate the antiviral activity of OAS1 p46.
source: Alternatively, viral interference of the OAS-RNase L pathway would negate the antiviral activity OAS1 p46.
evidence: Based on speculation about viral antagonism mechanisms.

claim: Mouse Hepatitis Virus and MERS-CoV accessory proteins encode a phosphodiesterase which degrades 2'−5'A.
source: Among positive sense RNA viruses Mouse Hepatitis Virus (MHV) and MERS-CoV accessory protein encodes for a phosphodiesterase which degrade 2'−5'A.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of viral antagonism mechanisms.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 does not carry a phosphodiesterase in its genome.
source: However, intriguingly, SARS-CoV-2 do not carry this phosphodiesterase in their genome, probably making them susceptible to OAS1 p46.
evidence: Based on knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 genome and inference about susceptibility.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is probably susceptible to OAS1 p46 because it lacks a phosphodiesterase.
source: However, intriguingly, SARS-CoV-2 do not carry this phosphodiesterase in their genome, probably making them susceptible to OAS1 p46.
evidence: Based on inference from lack of phosphodiesterase and in vitro antiviral data.

claim: Aggregation of several OAS1 proteins around viral dsRNA might increase the number of RNA-binding domains within the OAS1/vRNA complex.
source: Aggregation of several OAS1 proteins around viral dsRNA might also increase the number of RNA-binding domains within the OAS1/vRNA complex, thereby allowing access to longer vRNA which would increase 2′−5′A synthesis.
evidence: Based on speculation about oligomerization effects.

claim: OAS1 p46 proteins might oligomerize which is further aided by CaaX motif-mediated localization at Golgi membranes.
source: These data show p46 proteins might oligomerize which is further aided by CaaX motif-mediated localization at Golgi membranes.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing CFK mutant effects and membrane localization.

claim: The unique alternatively spliced C-terminal region including the oligomerization and prenylation motifs in p46 is maintained across vertebrates.
source: Together, we have defined features including the CaaX motif in the unique C-terminus that contribute to the enhanced antiviral activity of p46. The unique alternatively spliced C-terminal region including the oligomerization and prenylation motifs in p46 is maintained across vertebrates presumably because it displays the strongest antiviral activity compared to other OAS1 isoforms (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation data and inference about evolutionary selection.

claim: The unique C-terminal region of p46 is maintained across vertebrates presumably because it displays the strongest antiviral activity.
source: The unique alternatively spliced C-terminal region including the oligomerization and prenylation motifs in p46 is maintained across vertebrates presumably because it displays the strongest antiviral activity compared to other OAS1 isoforms (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on inference from conservation data and antiviral activity experiments.
